parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin -algia.
Borrowed from New Latin -ium, from Latin -um, based on Latin terms for metals, such as ferrum (“iron”).

parole.significato: -itis (denotes diseases characterized by inflammation, itself often caused by an infection)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin -ītis, from Ancient Greek -ῖτις (-îtis, “pertaining to”).
Borrowed from New Latin -tomia, from Ancient Greek τομία (tomía, “cutting”), from τέμνω (témnō, “to cut”).
Borrowed from New Latin abdōminālis.
Borrowed from New Latin abductor, from abdūcō + -tor.
Borrowed from New Latin abelmoschus, from Arabic حَبّ الْمِسْك (ḥabb al-misk, “pills of musk”).
Borrowed from New Latin Acalypha.
Borrowed from New Latin aphēlium, from Ancient Greek ἀπό (apó, “from, away from”) + ἥλιος (hḗlios, “the Sun”), modeled after apogaeum.
Borrowed from New Latin agallochum, from Ancient Greek ἀγάλοχον (agálokhon), ἀγάλλοχον (agállokhon), a loanword from a Middle Eastern language.
From New Latin allantois.

parole.significato: amblyopia (dimness or blurring of the eyesight)

parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin ametropia, from Ancient Greek ἄμετρος (ámetros) + ὤψ, ὠπός (ṓps, ōpós) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā).
Borrowed from New Latin anachronismus, from Ancient Greek ἀναχρονισμός (anakhronismós).
Borrowed from New Latin androecium.

parole.significato: anencephaly (birth defect involving the absence of the encephalon)
parole.testo: Internationalism. Learned borrowing from New Latin anencephalia. By surface analysis, an- + encefalia.
Borrowed from New Latin anosmia, from Ancient Greek ἀν- (an-) and ὀσμή (osmḗ, “smell”).
Borrowed from New Latin anthēra, from Ancient Greek ἀνθηρά (anthērá), feminine form of ἀνθηρός (anthērós, “flowery, blooming”) from ἄνθος (ánthos, “flower, blossom”).
Borrowed from New Latin anthrōpologia.
Borrowed from New Latin apnoea, from the Ancient Greek ἄπνοια (ápnoia).
Borrowed from New Latin apogaeus, from Ancient Greek ἀπόγειον (apógeion, “away from Earth”), from ἀπό (apó, “from, away from”) + γῆ (gê, “Earth”).

Borrowed from New Latin apophysis, from Ancient Greek ἀπόφυσις (apóphusis, “offshoot”), from ἀπό (apó, “off, from”) + φύσις (phúsis, “origin, birth”), from φύω (phúō, “to bring forth, to cause to grow”).
Learned borrowing from New Latin arborizāre.

Borrowed from New Latin archaismus, from Ancient Greek ἀρχαϊσμός (arkhaïsmós, “an antiquated phrase or style”), from ἀρχαίζω (arkhaízō, “to model one's style upon that of ancient writers”), from ἀρχαῖος (arkhaîos, “old, ancient”), from ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “beginning”), from ἄρχω (árkhō, “to begin”), from P
Borrowed from New Latin arrhythmia, from Ancient Greek ἄρρυθμος (árrhuthmos).
From New Latin artēriōla, from Ancient Greek ἀρτηρία (artēría) and -ola.
Borrowed from New Latin ascus, from Ancient Greek ἀσκός (askós, “bag, sack”).
Borrowed from New Latin assequibilis, from assequi, assequor (“to obtain”). Compare Catalan assequible.
Borrowed from New Latin asphyxia, from Ancient Greek ἀσφυξία (asphuxía, “stopping of the pulse”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + σφύξις (sphúxis, “pulse”).

Borrowed from New Latin asymptōta (līnea) (literally “line not meeting”), from Ancient Greek ἀσύμπτωτος (asúmptōtos, “not falling together”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + σύν (sún, “together”) + πτωτός (ptōtós, “apt to fall, fallen”), from πίπτω (píptō, “to fall”).
Borrowed from New Latin atmosphaera, from Ancient Greek ἀτμός (atmós, “vapor, steam”) + σφαῖρα (sphaîra, “sphere”).
Borrowed from New Latin autopsia, from Ancient Greek αὐτοψία (autopsía, “visual exam”).
Borrowed from New Latin Azalea, a genus name, from Ancient Greek ἀζαλέος (azaléos, “dry”), because the plant grows in dry soil.

parole.significato: bacterium (a single-celled organism with cell walls but no nucleus or organelles)
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin bacteria, plural of bactērium, from Ancient Greek βακτήριον (baktḗrion, “little rod”).
Borrowed from New Latin Batara.
Borrowed from New Latin biographia, based on Ancient Greek βίος (bíos, “life”).
Borrowed from New Latin bismutum, bismuthum, from German Wismut.
From New Latin borborygmus, from Ancient Greek βορβορυγμός (borborugmós), of onomatopoeic origin.
Borrowed from New Latin Brachiosaurus, from Ancient Greek βραχίων (brakhíōn, “arm”) + σαῦρος (saûros, “lizard”).
Borrowed from New Latin būbōnicus. By surface analysis, bubón (“bubo”) + -ico.
Borrowed from New Latin, from Latin butyrum, + -ico.
Borrowed from New Latin Bavarus.
Borrowed from New Latin cadmium.
Borrowed from New Latin Calla, former genus of the plant.

parole.significato: pot marigold (Calendula officinalis, a species of marigold)
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin calendula, from Latin kalendae, calendae, from calare (“to proclaim (the first day of a month was proclaimed in ancient Rome)”).
Borrowed from New Latin, named after Moravian botanist Joseph Kamel (‘Camellus’) (1661–1706). The Czech surname Kamel is a variant of Kamil.
Borrowed from New Latin Camelidae, from Latin camelus (“camel”).
Borrowed from New Latin Cantharida, from Latin canthăris.
Learned borrowing from New Latin Cartesiānus, from Cartesius.
Learned borrowing from New Latin carōtides, from Ancient Greek κᾰρωτῐ́δες (kărōtĭ́des).
Learned borrowing from New Latin catharticus, from Ancient Greek καθαρτικός (kathartikós).
Borrowed from New Latin coelacanthus, from Ancient Greek κοῖλος (koîlos, “hollow”) + ἄκανθα (ákantha, “spine”).
Borrowed from New Latin Coelenterata.
Borrowed from New Latin centrifugus, from Latin centrum (“center”) + fugiō (“to flee”).
Borrowed from New Latin centripetus, coined by Sir Isaac Newton, based on Latin centrum (“center”) + petō (“to seek”).
Borrowed from New Latin cercus, from Ancient Greek κέρκος (kérkos).
Borrowed from New Latin zerum, from Medieval Latin zephirum, from Andalusian Arabic صِفْر (ṣífr), from Classical Arabic صِفْر (ṣifr, “zero, nothing, empty, void”).
Borrowed from New Latin cervicālis, formed from the root of Latin cervix (“the neck, nape of the neck”) and -alis (see -al). Equivalent to cérvix + -al.
From New Latin chilensis, from Chile + -ēnsis.
Borrowed from New Latin zygōmaticus. By surface analysis, cigoma + -ático.
Borrowed from New Latin cirrhosis, from Ancient Greek κιρρός (kirrhós) + -σις (-sis).
From New Latin cōphōsis, from Ancient Greek κώφωσις (kṓphōsis).
Borrowed from New Latin collūtōrium, from collūtum, supine of colluere (“to wash thoroughly”).
Borrowed from New Latin compressor.
Borrowed from New Latin cottus, from Ancient Greek κόττος (kóttos).
Borrowed from New Latin cremātōrius, from cremō + -tōrius. By surface analysis, cremar + -torio.
Borrowed from New Latin cremātōrium, from cremō + -tōrium. By surface analysis, cremar + -torio.
Borrowed from New Latin chronologia, from Ancient Greek χρονολογία (khronología), from χρόνος (khrónos, “time”). By surface analysis, crono- + -logía.
Borrowed from New Latin quatriplicāre, from Latin quatri-, modelled on duplicāre (“double”), triplicāre (“triple”), etc.
Borrowed from New Latin Cambricus, from Latin Cambria (“Wales”).

parole.significato: position (of the body when lying down)
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin dēcubitus (“lying down”).
Borrowed from New Latin dēfenestrātiōnem, Latin dē (“from; out”) + fenestra (“window”) + -ātiō (suffix indicating an action or process).
Borrowed from New Latin dēlētērius, from Ancient Greek δηλητήριος (dēlētḗrios).
Learned borrowing from New Latin deltoideus. By surface analysis, delto- + -oide.
From New Latin dermatītis. By surface analysis, dermat- + -itis.
Borrowed from New Latin dīnosaurus, from Ancient Greek δεινός (deinós, “terrible, awesome”) + σαῦρος (saûros, “lizard”), + -io.
Borrowed from New Latin dīnosaurus.
From New Latin, from Ancient Greek δυσ- (dus-) + λᾰλῐᾱ́ (lălĭā́). By surface analysis, dis- + -lalia.
Learned borrowing from New Latin dyslexia.
From New Latin echolalia, from Ancient Greek ἠχώ (ēkhṓ, “echo”) and λαλιά (laliá, “talk, chat”). By surface analysis, eco- + -lalia.
Borrowed from New Latin edema, from Ancient Greek οἴδημα (oídēma, “swelling”), from οἰδέω (oidéō, “to swell”).
Borrowed from New Latin ēlectricus, from Latin ēlectrum, from Ancient Greek ἤλεκτρον (ḗlektron, “amber”).

parole.significato: embolism (obstruction or occlusion of a blood vessel by an embolus)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin embolismus. By surface analysis, émbolo + -ismo.
Borrowed from New Latin ēmulsiōnem, based on Latin ēmulgeō (“to milk out, extract”).

Borrowed from New Latin encyclopaedia, a false rendering of Ancient Greek ἐγκύκλιος (enkúklios, “circular”) (from ἐν (en, “in”) + κύκλος (kúklos, “circle”)) + παιδεία (paideía, “education”, literally “rearing of a child”), as "an all-around education", but literally "training in a circle". The moder
Internationalism. Learned borrowing from New Latin encephalon, from Ancient Greek ἐγκέφαλος (enképhalos, “within the head”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + κεφαλή (kephalḗ, “head”).
Borrowed from New Latin emphysēma, from Ancient Greek ἐμφύσημα (emphúsēma, “swelling, inflation”), from ἐμφυσάω (emphusáō, “to inflate”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + φυσάω (phusáō, “to blow”).
Borrowed from New Latin epithēlium.
From New Latin ecchymōsis, from Ancient Greek ἐκχύμωσις (ekkhúmōsis).
Borrowed from New Latin erythropoiesis, from Ancient Greek ἐρυθρο- (eruthro-, “red”) and ποίησις (poíēsis, “production”).
From New Latin scaphoides, from Ancient Greek σκαφοειδές (skaphoeidés), from σκάφη (skáphē, “boat”) + -ειδές (-eidés, “similar to”).
Borrowed from New Latin scandium, from Scandia, a contraction of Scandinavia, where minerals containing this element where found.
From New Latin spondylolisthēsis, equivalent to espondilo- + Ancient Greek ὀλισθάνω (olisthánō).
Borrowed from New Latin spora, from Ancient Greek σπορά (sporá, “sowing, seed”) or maybe from Frankish *sporo (“spur”).
Borrowed from New Latin sporangium, from Ancient Greek σπορά (sporá, “seed”) + ἀγγεῖον (angeîon, “vessel”).
Borrowed from New Latin staphisagria, from Ancient Greek σταφίς ἀγρίᾱ (staphís agríā, literally “wild grape”).
Borrowed from New Latin stalactītēs, from Ancient Greek σταλακτός (stalaktós) + New Latin -ītēs.
Borrowed from New Latin stalagmitēs, based on Ancient Greek σταλαγμός (stalagmós, “a dropping, dripping”) or στάλαγμα (stálagma, “drop”), from σταλάσσω (stalássō, “to let drop”).
Borrowed from New Latin stipulāris, from stipula (“stalk of hay”).

Borrowed from New Latin strabismus, from Ancient Greek στραβισμός (strabismós, “(action of) squinting”), from στραβίζω (strabízō, “to squint”), from στραβός (strabós, “squinting, squint-eyed”) (whence the synonymous Latin strabus), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *strebʰ-, whence Ancient Greek στρ
From New Latin stramonium.
Borrowed from New Latin staticus, from Ancient Greek στατικός (statikós).
Borrowed from New Latin Eucalyptus, from Ancient Greek εὖ (eû, “well”) + καλυπτός (kaluptós, “covered”).
Borrowed from New Latin euphoria, from Ancient Greek εὐφορία (euphoría), from εὔφορος (eúphoros, “bearing well”).
From New Latin exaeresis, from Ancient Greek ἐξαίρεσῐς (exaíresĭs, “a taking out, an extraction”).
Unadapted borrowing from New Latin factotum.
Borrowed from New Latin phacochoerus, from Ancient Greek φακός (phakós, “lens”) + χοῖρος (khoîros, “pig”).
Borrowed from New Latin phylum, from Ancient Greek φῦλον (phûlon, “race”).
Learned borrowing from New Latin focālis.
Borrowed from New Latin phorminx, from Ancient Greek φόρμιγξ (phórminx) First attested in 1792.
Borrowed from New Latin francium, alluding to Francia, France, country of its discoverer.
From New Latin fuchsia, eponym from Leonhart Fuchs.
Borrowed from New Latin physica (“physics”), from Ancient Greek φυσικός (phusikós, “natural”).

Learned borrowing from New Latin phōsphorus, from Ancient Greek φωσφόρος (phōsphóros, “torchbearer, light bearer”), from φῶς (phôs, “light”) + φέρω (phérō, “to carry, bear, bring”). Compare Sicilian pòspuru.
Borrowed from New Latin geneticus, from Latin genĕsis.
Borrowed from New Latin geneticus, from Latin genĕsis.
Borrowed from New Latin [Term?], from Ancient Greek γεωδαισία (geōdaisía, “division of the earth”).
Borrowed from New Latin glandulāris, from Latin glandula (“little acorn”).
Borrowed from New Latin gnomus, coined by Paracelsus as a synonym for pygmaeus (“pygmy”).
Borrowed from New Latin Gorgonia, from Latin Gorgō, from Ancient Greek Γοργώ (Gorgṓ).
Borrowed from New Latin gorilla, from Ancient Greek Γόριλλαι (Górillai).
Borrowed from New Latin gravitātiōnem. Equivalent to gravitar + -ción.
Borrowed from New Latin gravitāre, from Latin gravitās.
Borrowed from New Latin helium, from Ancient Greek ἥλιος (hḗlios, “sun”), because the element was first observed in the solar spectrum.
Borrowed from New Latin hypothermia, from Ancient Greek ὑπο- (hupo-, “under”) + θέρμη (thérmē, “heat”) + Latin -ia. By surface analysis, hipo- + -termia.
Borrowed from New Latin Hortensia, from Hortense de Beauharnais, from whom the flower is named after.
Borrowed from New Latin, from hyrax + -aceum.
Learned borrowing from New Latin īnfīnītēsimus. By surface analysis, infinito + -ésimo.
Borrowed from New Latin īnflōrēscentia, from Late Latin īnflōrēscō (“to be covered in flowers”).
Borrowed from New Latin īnfūsōrium, from Latin īnfūsus, perfect passive participle of īnfundō (“to pour in, to cause to absorb, to sprinkle”).
Borrowed from New Latin īridium, from Latin Īridem (“Iris, goddess of rainbows”), from Ancient Greek Ἶρις (Îris), due to the bright color of many of its salts; cf. also -io, element-forming suffix.
From New Latin isometria, from Ancient Greek. Equivalent to iso- + -metría.
From New Latin ischaemia, from Ancient Greek ἴσχαιμος (ískhaimos, “stoppage of blood flow”), from ῐ̓́σχω (ĭ́skhō, “to hold back, restrain; to stay, stop”) + αἷμᾰ (haîmă, “blood”).
Learned borrowing from New Latin Iēsūīta.

parole.significato: any species of the genus Lavandula
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin lavandula, itself from Italian lavanda (“lavender”).
Borrowed from New Latin lībellula, coined by Carl von Linné after lībella (“carpenter's level”), because of the insect's ability to stay level when hovering.
Borrowed from New Latin Lycaon.

Borrowed from New Latin lithium, from Ancient Greek λίθος (líthos, “stone”) + -io, to reflect the element's discovery in solid mineral, as opposed to potassium, discovered in plant ashes, and sodium, often found in animal blood.
Borrowed from New Latin latex (“clear fluid which is part of a humour or bodily fluid”), a later use of Latin latex (“water; liquid, fluid”).
From New Latin Marianus, from Latin Maria + -anus. Equivalent to María + -ano.
Borrowed from New Latin marsūpiālis, from Latin marsūpium "pouch", from Ancient Greek μαρσίππιον (marsíppion). More at marsupio.
Learned borrowing from New Latin mechanismus.
Learned borrowing from New Latin mediastīnum.
Borrowed from New Latin microscopium, from Ancient Greek μικρός (mikrós, “small”) + σκοπέω (skopéō, “to look at”), equivalent to micro- + -scopio.
Borrowed from New Latin minūtiōsus. Equivalent to minucia + -oso.
From New Latin myositis.
Internationalism, from New Latin myxōma. By surface analysis, mixo- + -oma.
Borrowed from New Latin molecula, diminutive of Latin moles (“mass”).
Borrowed from New Latin nasua, from Latin nāsus (“nose”).
Borrowed from New Latin neonātus, influenced by Italian neonato.
Calque of New Latin nervus vagus (literally “wandering nerve”).
Borrowed from New Latin neurologia. By surface analysis, neuro- + -logía.
Borrowed from New Latin nostalgia, coined from Ancient Greek νόστος (nóstos, “returning home”) + ἄλγος (álgos, “pain”).
Borrowed from New Latin occipitālis, from Latin occiput (“the back of the head”).
Borrowed from New Latin odontalgia, from Ancient Greek ὀδονταλγία (odontalgía, “toothache”), from ὀδών (odṓn, “tooth”) (genitive singular ὀδόντος (odóntos)) + ἄλγος (álgos, “pain”).
Borrowed from New Latin ophiūra (“brittle star”), from Ancient Greek ὄφις (óphis, “serpent”) + οὐρά (ourá, “tail”) (referring to the serpent-like arms of the brittle star).
From New Latin onychomantia, from Ancient Greek ὄνυξ (ónux), ὄνῠχος (ónŭkhos) + -mancia.
From New Latin onomantia, from Ancient Greek ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”) + -mancia.
Borrowed from New Latin oryctologia.
Borrowed from New Latin Orchideae, Orchidaceae, an irregular formation from Latin orchis, from Ancient Greek ὄρχις (órkhis, “orchid, testicle”).
Borrowed from New Latin parametrum (“parameter”), from Ancient Greek παρά (pará, “beside”) + μέτρον (métron, “measure”); see English meter.
Borrowed from New Latin pauciflōrus.
Borrowed from New Latin pedunculus.
From New Latin penumbra, from Latin paene (“almost”) + umbra (“shadow”).
Learned borrowing from New Latin peperomia, from Ancient Greek πέπερι (péperi, “pepper”) + ὅμοιος (hómoios, “similar, like”).
Borrowed from New Latin perianthium, from Ancient Greek περί (perí, “around”) + ἄνθος (ánthos, “flower”).

parole.significato: perihelion (the point in the elliptical orbit of a comet, planet, etc., where it is nearest to the Sun)
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin perihēlium, from Ancient Greek περί (perí, “around”) + ἥλιος (hḗlios, “the Sun”).
Borrowed from New Latin pertussis, from per- + tussi. Cf. tos.
Learned borrowing from New Latin periodus, a learned borrowing from Ancient Greek περῐ́οδος (perĭ́odos, “going round in a circle, periodic recurrence”).
Borrowed from New Latin pȳgidium, from Ancient Greek πῡγή (pūgḗ, “tail”).
Borrowed from New Latin placenta, from Latin placenta (“cake”), from Ancient Greek πλακόεντα (plakóenta), accusative of πλακόεις (plakóeis, “flat”).
Borrowed from New Latin plantigradus, from Latin planta + gradus, equivalent to planta + -i- + -grado.
Borrowed from New Latin polōnium, after Polōnia (“Poland”), Latin name of the homeland of Marie Curie, one of its discoverers and namers (the other being her husband Pierre Curie).

Borrowed from New Latin potassium, from English potassium, coined in 1807 by Humphrey Davy, from English potash, from Dutch potasch, from Middle Dutch pottaschen (literally “pot ashes”), ultimately derived from Proto-Germanic *puttaz (“pot”) and *askǭ (“ash”).
Borrowed from New Latin praseodymium, from German Praseodym, from Ancient Greek πράσιος (prásios, “leek-green”) (because of its green salts) + δίδυμος (dídumos, “twin”).
Borrowed from New Latin propāganda.
Borrowed from New Latin prosōdicus, from Ancient Greek προσῳδικός (prosōidikós), from προσῳδία (prosōidía, “song with accompaniment, tone or pitch of a word”). See prosodia.
From New Latin proteles, from Ancient Greek πρῶτος (prôtos) + τέλειος (téleios).
Borrowed from New Latin Protista, from Ancient Greek πρώτιστος (prṓtistos), corresponding to proto- + -ista.
Borrowed from New Latin primula.
Borrowed from New Latin psychologia, from Ancient Greek ψυχή (psukhḗ, “soul”) + -logia.
Borrowed from New Latin pupa, from special use of Latin pūpa.
From New Latin pemphigus, from Ancient Greek πέμφιξ (pémphix, “pustule”).
Learned borrowing from New Latin chiro-.
Borrowed from New Latin Ricinus communis, denoting the castor oil plant, thus cognate with ricino (“castor”).
Learned borrowing from New Latin rigor mortis (literally “stiffness of death”).
Borrowed from New Latin rhōtacismus.
Borrowed from New Latin rubidium, from Latin rubidus (“blonde”), because under spectroscopic analysis it has two red stripes; cf. also the element-forming suffix -io.
Borrowed from New Latin serpentārius.
Borrowed from New Latin silicium, from oblique cases of Latin silex (“flint”), which is a type of quartz and made of silica (silicon dioxide). Named in 1808 by Humphry Davy.

Borrowed from New Latin symbiosis, from Ancient Greek σῠμβῐ́ωσῐς (sŭmbĭ́ōsĭs, “a living together, companionship”), from συμβιόω (sumbióō, “to live together”), from συν- (sun-, “with”) + βῐ́ος (bĭ́os, “life”).
Borrowed from New Latin symptomaticus, from Ancient Greek συμπτωματικός (sumptōmatikós, “of or relating to a chance (or a symptom), casual”), from σύμπτωμα (súmptōma, “a symptom”).

Borrowed from New Latin synopticus, from Ancient Greek συνοπτικός (sunoptikós, “seeing the whole together or at a glance”), from σύνοψις (súnopsis, “a general view, synopsis”), from σύν (sún, “with”) + ὄψις (ópsis, “view”).
Borrowed from New Latin Sixtō-Clēmentīnus.
Borrowed from New Latin skua, from Faroese skúgvur/skúvur, from Old Norse skúfr.
Borrowed from New Latin sodium, from Italian soda, coined by H. Davy, 1778-1829, British physicist and chemist who discovered it.
Borrowed from New Latin sōrus, from Ancient Greek σωρός (sōrós, “heap”).
Borrowed from New Latin subluxāre.
Borrowed from New Latin suffruticem, from Latin frutex (“bush, shrub”). Cognate with English suffrutex and the Italian suffrutice.
Borrowed from New Latin suīcīdium, from suī (“oneself”) + -cīdium (“-cide”).
Borrowed from New Latin sepalum, a portmanteau coined in 1790 from sēparātus (“separate”) and petalum (“petal”).
Learned borrowing from New Latin tachycardia. By surface analysis, taqui- + -cardia.
Borrowed from New Latin tentāculum, from Latin tentō.

parole.significato: theodolite (surveying instrument used to measure horizontal and vertical angles)
parole.testo: From New Latin theodolitus; see theodolite.
Borrowed from New Latin tȳphus, from Ancient Greek τῦφος (tûphos, “fever, stupor”).
Borrowed from New Latin tyrannosaurus, from Ancient Greek τύραννος (túrannos, “tyrant”) + σαῦρος (saûros, “lizard”).
Borrowed from New Latin tomentosus.
From tos (“cough”) + ferina, feminine of ferino (“wild”).
Internationalism. Learned borrowing from New Latin trachōma.
Borrowed from New Latin tulipa, from Turkish tülbent (“fine muslin, turban”), from Persian دلبند (dolband, “turban”). Doublet of turbante.
Borrowed from New Latin thuja, from Ancient Greek θυία (thuía), an African tree that was formerly included in the genus.
From New Latin ūrachus, from Ancient Greek οὐραχός (ourakhós).
From New Latin uromantia, from Ancient Greek οὖρον (oûron, “urine”). Equivalent to uro- + -mancia.
Borrowed from New Latin urtīcāria, from Latin urtīca (“nettle”) + -āria.
Borrowed from New Latin varicella, a false diminutive of Medieval Latin variola (“pock, pustule”).
Borrowed from New Latin vasculāris.
Borrowed from New Latin valvula, diminutive of valva (“leaf of a door”).
From New Latin vēnula, from vēna and -ula.
Borrowed from New Latin xenia, from Ancient Greek ξενία (xenía, “hospitality”).
Borrowed from New Latin acarus, from Ancient Greek ἄκαρι (ákari, “cheese mite”), from ἀκαρής (akarḗs, “tiny”).
Borrowed from New Latin aphidem.
Learned borrowing from New Latin embolus, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἔμβολος (émbolos).

parole.significato: osmosis (movement of molecules across a membrane)
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin ōsmosis, from Koine Greek ὠσμός (ōsmós, “push, thrust”), from a contracted form of Ancient Greek ὠθισμός (ōthismós), ὠστισμός (ōstismós), from ὠθίζω (ōthízō, “to push, to thrust”), from ὠθέω (ōthéō, “to push”).
